description: Ren-Eh is a solo-bolo team by Xy
summary: Ulan, measured is an interactive data story and trend explorer that turns NASA Earth observations into evidence anyone can check. It maps 25 years (2001–2025) of GPM IMERG rainfall across 3,735 squares of the Philippines and tests every trend with Sen's slope and the Mann-Kendall test, so users see what is changing, where, by how much, and whether it is significant. It follows El Niño from the rain to the farms: in El Niño-start years, January to April rain fell 60% nationwide, crops were measurably less green at all 12 sampled farm sites (MODIS NDVI), and farm days ran hotter. An unsupervised machine-learning step (k-means) rediscovers PAGASA's four climate types from satellite data alone, explaining why the same El Niño takes a dry season from western Luzon but part of the wet season from the Pacific coast. The findings are cross-checked against NASA Giovanni. This matters because rainfall shapes the food and water supply of more than 110 million Filipinos.
details:
What it does

Ulan, measured ("ulan" is Filipino for rain) is a scrolling story with a live map, followed by an explorer. Its 16 chapters move from what is normal (average rain, record years, how much one year swings), through El Niño's effect on the January to April dry season, to the farms, and finally to long-term trends and which of them are statistically significant. In the explorer, users pick a variable (satellite rainfall, modelled air temperature or farm surface temperature), a time window and a view, then tap any rain square, region or farm site to see its time series, rate of change and significance test. Two guided demos teach the workflow, and a glossary defines every measurement.

Key findings and how significant they are

We rate each finding with a statistical test. Plain-language scale: very strong (p < 0.001), strong (p < 0.01), meets the test (p < 0.05), not significant (p >= 0.05). A p-value is how often a result this large would appear by chance alone.

1. El Niño dries the January to April season.

In the 9 years that began in El Niño, January to April rain averaged 269 mm against 668 mm in the other 16 years: 59.8% less. Significance: VERY STRONG. An exact permutation test, which tries all 2,042,975 ways of choosing 9 of the 25 years, gives p = 0.0000044. All 9 El Niño-start years fell below the January to April average (chance alone: p = 0.00003). All 17 regions were drier, and each region's gap is significant on its own (every p < 0.005; 16 of 17 survive a strict Bonferroni correction).

Caption: El Niño-start years averaged 59.8% less January to April rain (p = 0.0000044). Brown squares on the map had less rain in those years; almost the whole country is brown.

2. The data found four rain calendars.

An unsupervised k-means algorithm, given only each square's 12 monthly rain shares and no geography, sorted 3,735 squares into four groups that match the Philippine weather agency's (PAGASA) climate Types I to IV. Significance: this is a pattern-finding step, not a hypothesis test. It is fully reproducible: the browser and the data pipeline produce identical groups, checked square by square. It explains why one cause has different effects: El Niño removes 55 to 66% of January to April rain in every group, but for the Pacific coast (Type II) those months are 32% of the year's rain, part of its wet season.

Caption: The interactive k-means widget after 35 rounds. Each dot is one rain square; the map shows the four rain calendars it found, matching PAGASA climate Types I to IV.

3. Farms were drier, hotter and less green in El Niño-start years.

At 12 cropland sites: rain 60.7% lower (p = 0.00001), daytime surface 1.23 °C hotter (p = 0.000005), and crop greenness (MODIS NDVI) 0.035 lower (p = 0.000005), lower at all 12 sites (sign test p = 0.0005). Significance: VERY STRONG for all three. Night surface temperature showed no significant El Niño difference (p = 0.35).

Caption: Crop greenness (MODIS NDVI) at 12 cropland sites. Dark bars are El Niño-start years, almost all below the 25-year average.


4. Long-term trends: most rain changes could still be chance.

National rainfall rose 6.9% per decade over 2001-2025, but p = 0.168: NOT SIGNIFICANT with 25 years. Locally, 13.5% of land has a rise that meets the test, against about 5% expected by chance, and no square has a significant fall. Mimaropa (p = 0.047) and Calabarzon meet the test. With 45 years of independent CHIRPS data (1981-2025), the national annual rise becomes STRONG (p = 0.010), showing why longer records matter. Air temperature rose 0.26 °C per decade: VERY STRONG (p < 0.001), in all 17 regions.

Caption: Where the 25-year rainfall rise meets the Mann-Kendall test (p < 0.05): 13.5% of land, shown in solid teal. Faded squares could be chance.

5. Our numbers are checked.

NASA Giovanni, run on the same IMERG data, matches our year-to-year series (r = 0.976, p < 0.0000001) and our El Niño gap (-57.2% vs -59.8%). Independent CHIRPS data agrees (r = 0.991, gap -56.0%).

Caption: Our national January to April series (solid) against NASA Giovanni's (dashed), with El Niño-start years in yellow. The two lines track each other closely (r = 0.976).

6. The satellites saw what farmers reported.

We compared Department of Agriculture El Niño farm-damage reports in the news (2019 and 2024) with each named region's January to April rain. In 2024, 9 of the 11 damaged regions had at least 25% less rain; the two most damaged, Mimaropa (P1.7 billion) and Western Visayas (P1.5 billion), were our 4th and 2nd driest of 17 regions, and they contain the hardest-hit provinces, Palawan and Iloilo. In 2019, all 6 reported regions were 37% to 72% drier. Two 2024 regions, Davao Region and Soccsksargen, had near-normal rain, and the page says the rain record does not explain their damage. Significance: too few years for a formal test, so this is supporting context, not proof.

Caption: "Did the satellites see what farmers reported?" Department of Agriculture damage reports beside each region's January to April rain and dryness rank.

What did not hold up, and we say so: the farm-night warming trend (+0.26 °C per decade, p = 0.030) loses significance before Terra's orbit drift (p = 0.29) and is not confirmed by an orbit-free air-temperature check (p = 0.088). The small NDVI trend (p = 0.047) also fails the pre-drift refit (p = 0.73).

Method notes: trends use Sen's slope with the Mann-Kendall test (two-sided, tie-corrected). El Niño gaps use exact two-sided permutation tests. Both treat years as independent and do not adjust for autocorrelation. Significance shows association, not cause.

How it works

A Python pipeline downloads every dataset from credential-free NASA services and pins each response with its URL, retrieval time and SHA-256 hash, so an offline rebuild reproduces the site's data byte for byte. Every sentence in the story is generated from the computed results, and the build fails if a sentence's wording contradicts its number. The website is static: the browser never calls NASA.

Data

NASA GPM IMERG Final Run rainfall and MERRA-2 air temperature (via NASA POWER); MODIS land cover, land surface temperature and NDVI (via ORNL DAAC); NASA Giovanni; NOAA's Oceanic Niño Index; geoBoundaries borders; and CHIRPS rainfall via the KNMI Climate Explorer.

Creativity

An interactive k-means widget lets users press Step and watch the algorithm sort 3,735 squares into rain calendars while the map repaints in real time. The farm chain links several variables into one story: less rain, hotter days, less-green crops.

Why it matters

The strongest signal in 25 years of NASA rain over the Philippines is El Niño's, and the page shows how to tell it apart from slow trends that 25 years cannot yet confirm.

For students: they pick a variable, a place and a time window and run the same tests scientists use, and they see a strong signal, a trend that could be chance, and a result that fell apart under checking, side by side. A k-means model they can step through shows machine learning finding PAGASA's climate types from rain data alone.

For scientists: every NASA response is pinned with its URL, retrieval time and SHA-256 hash so the analysis rebuilds offline byte for byte; the results are cross-checked against NASA Giovanni and independent data; and negative results are reported, not dropped. It shows how 0.1° IMERG rain, MODIS greenness and MERRA-2 temperature can track El Niño's farm impacts region by region.

For farms and planners: El Niño's dry-season signal is large, consistent and visible a season ahead in the ocean index, it matches where farm damage was reported, and national air temperature is rising 0.26 °C per decade, a trend that meets the test.

Caption: The site's "Why it matters" section: El Niño's signal (p = 0.0000044) set against a national rain trend that 25 years cannot yet confirm (p = 0.168).

Factors we considered

We replaced a data source that failed an audit (MERRA-2 rainfall gave 2.3 times IMERG in 2020), refit trends before Terra's orbit drift, and report findings that did not hold up. We also considered accessibility, phone-width layouts, reduced motion, and keeping the site free of NASA branding.

Tools

TypeScript, Astro, MapLibre GL JS and Zod for the website; Python with NumPy and Shapely for the data pipeline; Bun and Python unittest for tests; Playwright, VHS and ffmpeg for the demo videos; Cloudflare Workers for hosting.

Use of SI

The code, data processing, tests, documentation, demo videos and screenshots were produced with Claude Code (Claude Opus 5.5) under my direction and reviewed by me; I take ownership of them. This is disclosed in the README, the project metadata, and watermarks on every video and screenshot.
